reason: The sources reliably support over 15 distinct, double-sourced claims detailing the extreme engineering, dimensions, and deployment of the JWST sunshield.
story: The James Webb Space Telescope operates in deep space to detect faint infrared heat signals from the early universe. To see these faint targets, the telescope must stay colder than minus 370 degrees Fahrenheit. To achieve this without active coolants, NASA and its partners built a massive five-layer sunshield roughly the size of a tennis court. Made of ultra-thin Kapton coated with aluminum and silicon, its layers are thinner than a human hair—the front layer is just 0.05 millimeters thick, while its protective metal coatings are measured in nanometers. Folded inside an Ariane 5 rocket for launch on Christmas Day 2021, the sunshield required a nerve-wracking sequence of 139 release mechanisms, 90 cables, and 400 pulleys to unfurl in space. Completed on January 4, 2022, the successful deployment retired over 70 percent of the mission's 344 single-point failures, creating a thermal barrier between a scorching hot side and a deep-freeze cold side.
angle: A tennis-court-sized sunshield with layers thinner than a human hair keeps one side of the Webb telescope at 230 degrees Fahrenheit while the other sits at minus 390 degrees.

claims.claim: The James Webb Space Telescope's sunshield is roughly the size of a tennis court.
The sunshield consists of five distinct layers of heat-reflecting material.
The sunshield layers are primarily made of Kapton polyimide film.
All five layers of the sunshield are coated on both sides with aluminum to reflect heat.
The outermost sun-facing layers have a doped-silicon coating that gives them a purple or lavender-pink color.
The sunshield protects the telescope optics by blocking light and heat from the Sun, Earth, and Moon.
The telescope optics and instruments must be kept under 50 Kelvin (minus 370 degrees Fahrenheit) to detect faint infrared signals.
The sunshield was folded to fit inside the nose cone of an Ariane 5 rocket for launch.
The James Webb Space Telescope launched into space on December 25, 2021.
Full deployment and tensioning of all five sunshield layers was successfully completed in space on January 4, 2022.
Ground testing in 2018 caused accidental tears in the sunshield membranes, contributing to launch delays.
The sunshield layer facing the sun is 0.05 millimeters (0.002 inches) thick, while the other four layers are 0.025 millimeters (0.001 inches) thick.
The aluminum coating on the sunshield layers is approximately 100 nanometers thick and the silicon coating is approximately 50 nanometers thick.
Unfurling and deploying the sunshield involved 139 release mechanisms, 70 hinge assemblies, 8 deployment motors, 90 cables, and roughly 400 pulleys.
Successfully deploying the sunshield retired approximately 70 to 75 percent of the telescope's 344 single-point failures.
Thermal Spot Bonding creates a grid pattern of rip-stops on each layer to prevent accidental tears from expanding.
When fully deployed, the sunshield measures approximately 21 meters long by 14 meters wide.

disputed: Sunshield width dimensions vary slightly across sources: S1, S2, S3, and S4 list dimensions around 21 m by 14 m (approx. 69.5 ft by 46.5 ft), whereas S6 lists width as 54 feet (16 m). Script should state 'roughly 21 by 14 meters' or 'tennis-court sized'.
Exact percentage of single-point failures retired: S5 quotes a tweet saying 'about 75%', whereas S6 attributes '70 to 75 percent' to project manager Bill Ochs. Script should state 'over 70 percent'.
